accepted.question_text: Let B = {B(s, t)}_{s,t >= 0} be a d-dimensional Brownian sheet, and for each fixed s > 0 consider the zero set of the slice along s, namely B^{-1}{0} intersect ({s} x (0, infinity)) = {t > 0 : B(s, t) = 0}. When d is 2 or 3, Theorem 1.2 shows that this slice-zero set has Hausdorff dimension 0 simultaneously for all s > 0. Is there a stronger topological statement: outside a single null set, is B^{-1}{0} intersect ({s} x (0, infinity)) actually a finite set for every s > 0?

evidence.quote: Theorem 1.2. If d in {2 , 3}, then the following holds outside a single P-null set: dim_H(B^{-1}{0} cap ({s} x (0 , infinity))) = 0 for all s > 0.
Open Problem 1. Suppose d in {2 , 3}. Is it true that outside a single null set, B^{-1}{0} cap ({s} x (0 , infinity)) is a finite set for all s > 0?

accepted.question_text: For a d-dimensional Brownian sheet B with d in {4, 5}, define Y_d(s) = {(t_1, t_2) in R_+^2 : B(s, t_1) = B(s, t_2)}, the set of double-point time pairs occurring in the slice along s. The global double-point sets D-hat_d and D-bar_d have positive dimensions given in equation (8.1). Must every individual slice nevertheless remain dimensionless in the sense that, outside a single null set, dim_H Y_d(s) = 0 for all s >= 0?

evidence.quote: Theorem 5.1 and a codimension argument together imply that with probability one, dim_H D-hat_d = (3 - d/2)^+, and dim_H D-bar_d = 2 wedge (3 - d/2)^+.

Open Problem 2. Define, for all s >= 0, Y_d(s) := {(t_1, t_2) in R_+^2 : B(s , t_1) = B(s , t_2)}. Then is it the case that if d in {4 , 5} then, outside a single null-set, dim_H Y_d(s) = 0 for all s >= 0?

accepted.question_text: For a d-dimensional Brownian sheet B with d in {4, 5}, keep Y_d(s) = {(t_1, t_2) in R_+^2 : B(s, t_1) = B(s, t_2)} as the set of double-point time pairs in the slice along s. Is there a topological strengthening of the previous question analogous to Open Problem 1: outside a single null set, is Y_d(s) a finite set for every s > 0?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 2. Define, for all s >= 0, Y_d(s) := {(t_1, t_2) in R_+^2 : B(s , t_1) = B(s , t_2)}.
Open Problem 1 has the following analogue for double-points. Open Problem 3. Let d in {4 , 5}. Then is it true that outside a single null set, Y_d(s) is a finite set for all s > 0?

accepted.question_text: For the zero set B^{-1}{0} of a d-dimensional Brownian sheet, Theorem 1.1 shows that the fixed orthogonal projection onto the x-axis has the same Hausdorff dimension 2 - d/2 as B^{-1}{0} itself. Does this remain true for every random orthogonal projection as well? Equivalently, is there any random orthogonal projection for which the projection of B^{-1}{0} has Hausdorff dimension different from 2 - d/2?
accepted.context_brief: Random projections of the zero set

evidence.quote: Consequently, when d in {2 , 3}, the [Hausdorff] dimension of Z_d is equal to 2 - (d/2). Oddly enough, this is precisely the dimension of B^{-1}{0} as well; see Rosen [29, 30]. But Z_d is the projection of B^{-1}{0} onto the x-axis.

Marstrand [21] proved that almost every lower-dimensional orthogonal projection of a Borel set A has the same Hausdorff dimension as A. Theorem 1.1 proves that a given projection (say, onto the x-axis) of the zero-set of Brownian sheet has the same 'Marstrand property.'
Open Problem 4. Is there a (random) orthogonal projection such that the said projection of B^{-1}{0} has a different Hausdorff dimension than 2 - (d/2)?

accepted.question_text: Let u = (u_1, ..., u_d) solve a system of nonlinear hyperbolic stochastic PDEs with multiplicative noise of the form partial^2 u_i / (partial t partial x) = b_i(u) + sigma_i(u) dot B-hat, under reasonable boundary conditions, where sigma : R^d -> R^d is bounded, C^infinity, and strongly elliptic. For the additive-noise case, the law of u is mutually absolutely continuous with respect to that of a d-dimensional Brownian sheet, so the slice and hitting results of the paper transfer to u. Does the same family of results continue to hold for this multiplicative-noise system?
accepted.context_brief: Brownian-sheet slice theory for nonlinear SPDEs

evidence.quote: Consider d independent, two-dimensional white noises, B-dot_1, ..., B-dot_d, together with the following system of d non-interacting stochastic PDEs with additive noise: For a fixed T > 0, partial^2 u_i / (partial t partial x)(t , x) = B-hat_i(t , x) + b_i(u(t , x)).

Then, as long as b := (b_1, . . . , b_d) is bounded and Borel-measurable the law of the process u := (u_1, . . . , u_d) is mutually absolutely continuous with respect to the law of the two-parameter, d-dimensional Brownian sheet B. See Proposition 1.6 of Nualart and Pardoux [24]. Therefore, the theorems of the preceding sections apply to the process u equally well.

Open Problem 5. Suppose sigma : R^d -> R^d is a strongly elliptic, bounded, C^infinity function. Is it the case that the results of the previous sections apply to the solution of (partial^2 u_i/partial t partial x) = b_i(u) + sigma_i(u) dot B-hat with reasonable boundary conditions?

accepted.question_text: Consider the linear parabolic stochastic PDE system partial u_i / partial t (t, x) = partial^2 u_i / partial x^2 (t, x) + B-hat_i(t, x) with reasonable boundary conditions, where B-dot_1, ..., B-dot_d are independent space-time white noises. Is there a theory of slices along fixed times t for this parabolic system that parallels the Brownian-sheet slice results proved in the paper, such as the analysis of zeros, double points, and exceptional slices?

evidence.quote: Finally, we end with an open-ended question about parabolic SPDEs, about which we know far less at this point in time. We will state things about the additive linear case only. This case seems to be sufficiently difficult to analyse at this point in time.

Open Problem 6. Consider the following system of linear parabolic SPDE: partial u_i / partial t (t , x) = partial^2 u_i / partial x^2 (t , x) + B-hat_i(t , x), with reasonable boundary conditions. Is there an analysis of the 'slices' of u along different values of t that is analogous to the results of the present paper?
